# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is the most informative document in the series. It resolves the long-term outcomes and measurement questions left open by the earlier four, and its corrections of the comment and the meta-analysis are mostly justified. But it has one problem it doesn't mention: two control offices changed their meeting practices partway through the follow-up. It also states its two headline findings, the decline and the mediation result, more firmly than its own data support.

## Arithmetic: consistent

- **Varden per-hour gains:**
  - Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%**.
  - System logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%**.
- **Per-hour confidence intervals** are symmetric on the log scale. The output-per-FTE interval (±4.6) is symmetric on the linear scale, as at nine months.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, and 0.968 / 0.866 = **+11.8%**.
- **"Declined by about a quarter":** 12.5% → 9.8% on the same measure is a 22% decline, so "about a quarter" is fair.

## What it does well

- **It answers questions raised in earlier reviews.**
  - It uses system-log hours to capture unclaimed work.
  - It reports appeal overturn rates at 24 months, which is long enough for appeals to work through (3.2% vs 3.0%).
  - It reports baseline meeting time for both arms.
  - It finally pre-registers the meetings test.
- **It checks the meta-analysis's claim.** It looked up the four long-follow-up studies and found what was suspected in my review of the meta-analysis: all four are uncontrolled and use scheduled hours.
- **It keeps the cancelled counter arm in the report.** It explains why the arm was stopped and gives the cost implication, so the failure isn't hidden.
- **It treats the Halden survivors frankly**, flagging selection bias and the lack of a comparison group.
- **It doesn't overinterpret the unplanned observation.** It states that the trial cannot separate "reorganising alone" from "the hours cut forcing the reorganisation."

## Issues

**1. Two control offices changed practice, which affects the decline estimate.**
- In month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit." Their output per hour then rose 4.1%.
- In a difference-in-differences design, a rise in control output per hour shrinks the estimated treatment effect.
- So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control arm improving, not the treated arm's gain fading.
- Rough illustration: two of seven control offices improving by about 4% would raise the control average by about 1 percentage point. That is a large share of the 2.7-point decline.
- The paper reports the audit only as evidence that gains might be possible without cutting hours. It doesn't recognise that the audit contaminates its own estimate.
- **Needed:** a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or excluding months 15–24 for them. It should also state whether other control offices changed practices. Control staff knew about the trial, and the meetings finding had been published.

**2. The summary compares figures on different measures, and the decline isn't tested.**
- The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure.
- The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%. The text in §3 gets this right; the summary does not.
- The two intervals overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2), and the change between them is never tested.
- "The gain has therefore declined" should be weakened to something like "the point estimate is lower, consistent with partial fading or with change in the control arm."
- The core finding stands either way. The gain did not vanish around month ten, so the energy-extrapolation argument fails.

**3. The mediation result is described more firmly than its own limitations section allows.**
- **"Confirms" is too strong.** The limitations admit the analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. Mediation in a cluster trial estimates a mechanism under assumptions; it does not confirm one.
- **Registered is not the same as replicated.** The test uses the same seven treated offices that produced the unregistered hypothesis. Registration rules out flexible analysis choices, but this is not an independent test.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measurements of the same offices, not independent units. A 28–66% interval with seven offices per arm should be checked against a method that accounts for so few clusters.
- **Part of the meetings pathway is close to accounting.**
  - Meeting hours are part of total hours. Cutting low-output hours raises output per hour almost by definition.
  - A rough calculation suggests output per non-meeting hour barely changed. It assumes control offices at about 37.9 hours, of which 7.0 are meetings, and treated offices about 11% lower at around 33.7, of which 3.9 are meetings.
  - Non-meeting hours then fall only ~3.5%, about the same as output (−3.4%), so output per non-meeting hour is roughly unchanged.
  - That fits the paper's interpretation: the gain comes largely from removing low-value time. But "47% explained by meetings" and "18% by fatigue" are different kinds of claim, and the table presents them as parallel.
- **The two mediators probably interact.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. The paper doesn't say how shared variance was allocated between them.
- **The source of baseline meeting data needs explaining.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected in month six. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 treated, 7.2 control). Were these retrieved from calendar archives after the fact? It matters, because the earlier review's main concern was the lack of a baseline.

**4. The Halden follow-up.**
- **The baseline may be the wrong group's.** 40.3 hours is exactly the baseline Varga and Holm reported for their 27 time-tracking organisations. Is it also the baseline for these particular 11? If it was borrowed from the larger group, the +11.8% figure is not reliable.
- **There are three stages of selection, not two.** Organisations had to complete the pilot, continue afterwards, and agree to provide data (14 of 23 did).
- **"Upper bound" is plausible, not guaranteed.** Without a comparison group, general economic conditions could move the estimate in either direction.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the dichotomy.** The meta-analysis's coding would class it as discretionary, yet it reverted, citing client deadlines. The summary groups it under "client-facing or coverage obligations," but responsiveness to client deadlines is arguably a third category. It is an honest data point that should complicate the discretionary/coverage-bound split, not be absorbed into it.

**5. Items still missing from the earlier requests.**
- Backlog size, time-to-decision and compliance with statutory deadlines.
- Cost per case, including any overtime pay.
- Confidence intervals and difference-in-differences estimates for sick days and resignations, which are still reported as levels.
- How the counter arm's "+12% staff, +9% cost per contact" figures were derived. On the trial's own numbers, 12% more staff at full pay would suggest a cost rise closer to 12–13%, unless contacts handled also rose.

**6. Smaller points.**
- **Conflicts of interest.** The authors are evaluating their own trial and, through Okafor, the Halden pilot. They also designed the mediation test that vindicates their earlier hypothesis. Registration mitigates this, but it should be acknowledged.
- **Novelty and Hawthorne effects.** Two years largely rules out a short-term novelty effect. It does not rule out effects that persist while staff know they are being evaluated, and evaluation continued throughout.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Is there a per-hour gain under strict measurement? | **Yes, probably.** About 8.5% (3.4–13.8) at 24 months: randomised design, record-based output, log hours, discretionary work, one employer |
| Does it fade? | **Possibly partly.** The point estimate fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, but the change is untested and partly confounded by the control offices' meeting audit |
| Is the "entirely an artifact" claim right? | **No**, for discretionary work in this setting |
| Is the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim right? | **Unsupported.** It rested on four uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours |
| Does it work in coverage-bound work? | **No** at current staffing. The Varden counter arm was stopped, and restoring service would raise costs |
| Mechanism | **Removing low-value time (meetings) is the leading candidate**, partly by accounting; fatigue contributes less; about a third is unexplained. Not yet independently replicated |
| Could the gain be had without cutting hours? | **Open.** Suggested by two uncontrolled offices; needs a trial arm that reorganises without reducing hours |

If useful, I can draft a referee report on this field report, sketch a three-arm design (reduced hours, reorganisation only, control) to address the last open question, or write a synthesis across all five documents.
